title: Weather station
content_html:
Materials

  • Arduino Uno R3 (or compatible) — x1 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor module (3-pin breakout with onboard pull-up resistor) — x1 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 16x2 LCD Display with I2C backpack module (address usually 0x27 or 0x3F) — x1 (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • Half-size or full-size breadboard (400/830 points) — x1 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • Jumper wires, male-to-male and male-to-female, assorted pack — x1 pack (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • USB Type-A to Type-B cable (for Uno) — x1 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • Optional: Piezo buzzer (for extension challenge) — x1 (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • Optional: 220Ω resistor + LED (for status-light extension) — x1 each (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • Laptop with Arduino IDE installed — x1 per team

How It Works

This project builds a simple digital weather station. It has two main jobs: sensing the weather and showing the results on a screen.

The DHT11 sensor is a tiny device that can feel two things at once: how hot the air is (temperature) and how much water vapour is floating in the air (humidity). Instead of sending this information as a simple voltage, it sends it as a fast pattern of electrical pulses along a single wire — a bit like Morse code. The Arduino "listens" to this pattern using a special library (a pre-written set of instructions) that knows how to translate the pulses back into numbers we understand, like "24°C" and "60% humidity".

The LCD screen shows these numbers so we don't need a computer to see the results. Normally, a 16x2 LCD needs many wires to control it. To save wires, we use an I2C backpack — a small add-on board glued to the back of the LCD. I2C is a shared communication system that lets many devices talk to the Arduino using just two wires: SDA (data) and SCL (clock/timing). Each device on the I2C line has its own "address" (like a house number) so the Arduino knows exactly which device it's talking to — in this case, the LCD's address is usually 0x27 or 0x3F.

Every couple of seconds, the Arduino asks the DHT11 for a fresh reading, then writes the new temperature and humidity values onto the LCD screen, effectively logging live weather data in the room.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Lay out all components on the table and identify the DHT11 module's three pins: + (VCC), out (data/signal), and - (GND). Identify the LCD's four I2C pins: GND, VCC, SDA, SCL.
  2. Insert the DHT11 module and the breadboard rails as needed. Connect DHT11 VCC to Arduino 5V, DHT11 GND to Arduino GND, and DHT11 data/out pin to Arduino digital pin 2.
  3. Connect the LCD's I2C backpack: VCC to Arduino 5V, GND to Arduino GND, SDA to Arduino A4, and SCL to Arduino A5. (On some Uno boards, SDA/SCL are also broken out near the AREF pin — either works.)
  4. Double-check all wiring before powering on. Ask students to trace each wire out loud and say what it does — this builds understanding, not just muscle memory.
  5. Open the Arduino IDE. Go to Tools > Manage Libraries and install: "DHT sensor library" by Adafruit, "Adafruit Unified Sensor", and "LiquidCrystal I2C" (by Frank de Brabander or similar, whichever compiles cleanly).
  6. Paste in the full code provided below. Check the DHT_PIN (2), DHTTYPE (DHT11), and the LCD address (0x27) match your hardware.
  7. Upload the code to the Arduino. Watch the LCD backlight turn on and, after a few seconds, display "Temp: xx C" and "Hum: xx %".
  8. Open the Serial Monitor (baud rate 9600) to see the same readings printed as text — useful for logging or copying data into a spreadsheet.
  9. Have students gently breathe onto the DHT11 sensor and watch the humidity reading rise on the LCD within a couple of seconds.
  10. Have students cup their hand around the sensor (without touching the electronics) and observe the temperature reading slowly increase.
  11. If the LCD shows nothing or garbled characters, run an "I2C scanner" sketch (freely available online) to find the correct address, then update it in the code.
  12. Discuss with students why the readings update every 2 seconds instead of instantly (see Discussion Questions).

Full Code


#include <Wire.h>              // Library for I2C communication (talks to the LCD)
#include <LiquidCrystal_I2C.h> // Library that controls the I2C LCD screen
#include <DHT.h>               // Library that understands DHT11 sensor signals

#define DHTPIN 2       // The Arduino digital pin connected to the DHT11 data pin
#define DHTTYPE DHT11  // Tell the library which DHT model we are using

DHT dht(DHTPIN, DHTTYPE);        // Create a DHT sensor object on the chosen pin
LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2); // Create LCD object: I2C address 0x27, 16 columns, 2 rows

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);   // Start Serial Monitor communication at 9600 bits per second
  dht.begin();          // Initialise the DHT11 sensor
  lcd.init();           // Initialise the LCD screen
  lcd.backlight();      // Turn on the LCD backlight so we can see the text

  lcd.setCursor(0, 0);        // Move cursor to column 0, row 0 (top-left)
  lcd.print("Weather Station"); // Show a welcome message
  delay(2000);                // Pause 2 seconds so students can read it
  lcd.clear();                // Clear the screen before showing live data
}

void loop() {
  float humidity = dht.readHumidity();       // Ask the sensor for humidity (%)
  float temperature = dht.readTemperature();  // Ask the sensor for temperature (Celsius)

  // Check if either reading failed (DHT11 sometimes misses a beat)
  if (isnan(humidity) || isnan(temperature)) {
    Serial.println("Failed to read from DHT11 sensor!"); // Print error to Serial Monitor
    lcd.setCursor(0, 0);
    lcd.print("Sensor error!"); // Show error message on LCD too
    delay(2000);                // Wait before trying again
    return;                     // Skip the rest of this loop and try again
  }

  // Print readings to the Serial Monitor for logging/debugging
  Serial.print("Humidity: ");
  Serial.print(humidity);
  Serial.print(" %  Temperature: ");
  Serial.print(temperature);
  Serial.println(" C");

  // Display temperature on the top row of the LCD
  lcd.setCursor(0, 0);       // Column 0, row 0
  lcd.print("Temp: ");
  lcd.print(temperature, 1); // Print with 1 decimal place
  lcd.print(" C   ");        // Extra spaces clear leftover characters from longer numbers

  // Display humidity on the bottom row of the LCD
  lcd.setCursor(0, 1);       // Column 0, row 1
  lcd.print("Hum:  ");
  lcd.print(humidity, 1);
  lcd.print(" %   ");

  delay(2000); // DHT11 can only be read reliably about once every 2 seconds
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
LCD backlight is on but shows no text or only blocksWrong I2C address, or contrast not set correctly on non-backpack LCDsRun an I2C scanner sketch to find the correct address (commonly 0x27 or 0x3F) and update it in code
Serial Monitor prints "Failed to read from DHT11 sensor!" repeatedlyLoose wiring, wrong data pin defined in code, or DHT11 read too frequentlyCheck all three DHT11 connections, confirm DHTPIN matches the physical wire, ensure delay(2000) is present
Readings never change even when breathing on the sensorCode is stuck showing old error message, or sensor is faultyReset the Arduino, verify wiring, try swapping in a different DHT11 module to isolate the fault
Compile error: "DHT.h: No such file or directory"Required library not installedInstall "DHT sensor library" and "Adafruit Unified Sensor" via Library Manager, then re-upload
LCD shows random symbols or boxes instead of readable textLoose SDA/SCL connection, or LCD library version mismatchReseat jumper wires on A4/A5, confirm correct LiquidCrystal_I2C library is installed, re-upload code

Discussion Questions

  • Why does the DHT11 need at least 2 seconds between readings instead of updating instantly?
  • What jobs or situations in real life depend on knowing accurate temperature and humidity?
  • How do you think two wires (SDA and SCL) can control an entire screen full of letters?
  • If you left this weather station outside in the rain, what problems might happen, and how could you protect it?
  • Why might a professional weather station use a more expensive sensor than the DHT11?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a buzzer that beeps whenever the temperature rises above a chosen value (e.g. 28°C), using an if statement in the loop.
  • Medium: Use the millis() function to print a running "time since
